utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Yesterday you testified that you were a courier for a unit that was commanded by your brother, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of April, 1992, did that unit become a unit of the Territorial Defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly, but I guess to think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that on the 17th of April, 1992, the Serb side requested that you hand down your weapons and that you refused it.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the witness please wait before answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the Crisis Staff was located at the time.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my brother's house, that is, on that unit of that group of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you said that the Serb side attacked you on the 20th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was that unit performing a combat task at the time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was your unit defending itself on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not on the front lines, so we were not defending ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you were armed, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of April, did you leave as a courier to warn your brother of the presence of Serb forces which you had seen through your binoculars?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion were you captured?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After your capture, did a man in civilian clothes come up and say that the prisoners should not be tied and that you, as an invalid, should be allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So why did they keep you in spite of that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did they keep you because your brother was a commander of a TO unit?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. Nobody told me anything. They simply put me together with all the others, with other neighbours of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when asked by my learned friend you gave some detail about your capture, that some members of those Serb forces forced you to eat grass.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Then why didn't you mention this in either of your statements to the OTP investigators or in your statement to the Public Security Station in Sarajevo, although you did mention that instance?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, perhaps I forgot. I don't know, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified that from your neighbour you learnt at a later date that on that occasion some people, some men, were killed?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some ten or maybe 11, thereabouts. We thought that ten were killed, but 13 are missing, so 13 must have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did it happen in the village of Dzidzevo?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And which neighbour told you that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my friend, my neighbour, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we hear his name?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Sefik Spirjan, who was captured and was with me in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat, because in the transcript we cannot see the name? Perhaps the interpreter did not hear it. Could you please repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sefik Spirjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me in the camp in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you in the same room?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not, but we communicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us, how did you communicate?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we wrote on the glass, from the adjacent part of the camp, letters, and that is how we read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And under the roofs of the house in the KP Dom, were you allowed to approach the window panes and look through the window?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were allowed to do that after, after St. Vitus Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And from what distance could you watch this pane, window pane on which the message was written?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not written on the window pane. There was no message there on the window pane, but letter by letter was written by hand, and that is how we could read it. And the distance was about 15, maybe 20 metres. I wouldn't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And what room was he in at the time, that friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 18, and I was in 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that in an illustrated magazine which comes out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, an individual who kept a diary about those events wrote that five persons were killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not read that. Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the village of Dzidzevo.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not five, there were more than ten. I'm positive between ten and 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement to the OTP investigators, did you say that the SDA armed the Muslim people in part, and that they even had some pieces of artillery?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I shall repeat it. Did you tell the OTP investigators in your statement that the SDA armed the Muslim people, and that Muslims even had some pieces of artillery?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got a few rifles and that is all. I know nothing about the artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But did the SDA arm the Muslim people, did you say that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, true. We did get some weapons from the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that -- do you know if in 1992 in Foca or around it, a JNA unit was stationed perhaps at that time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you said that the Serb people were not afraid in 1992 because there was the JNA, and the Muslims were afraid. Now, since you tell us that there were no JNA units there, does that mean that Serbs were also afraid in the area of Foca?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that there were no JNA units, but that I did not -- was not aware of them since I am three and a half kilometres from Foca, and therefore I did not know what was going on in Foca because I could not move around. I was too afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday when asked by my learned friend you testified that after your capture on the bridge next to a place called Brod, on the road you saw written "This is Serbia." Why didn't you mention that in none [as translated] of your previous written statements?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why I didn't, but I am positive that that was -- that that is what the inscription said. And there were also flags.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did speak about those flags, but not about that sentence.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mistake, slip of my memory, but that is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After you arrived in KP Dom on the 20th of April, 1992, did the persons who admitted you there want to release you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, me and a 16-year-old lad.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So why did they decide to keep you after all?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the officer or whatever he was, when he came back, returned and asked me if I was Roko's brother, and I said, "I am." And then I don't know why they kept me after that. And this lad also stayed with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was it an army officer?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in a uniform, and since I never served in the army, I can't distinguish various ranks. All I know is that he had a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you said that after you arrived in the KP Dom you were put in an isolation cell where there were 15 of you, and that is another thing that you failed to mention when you spoke earlier about your capture and imprisonment. Could you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain it. I made quite a number of statements, and it was as I said. And why I did not say that, well, I cannot really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I stand by every statement I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you told the Court how Mr. Djuric, Kajgana, and Kovacevic were beaten. Was that on the 26th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 26th? No, not then. It was before that. It could have been 22nd, 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The soldiers who were still in the prison beat the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness did not answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Until when were those soldiers in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until about the 25th, I think; a day before or a day after - I don't know - but around the 25th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, either the witness spoke very quietly or nobody heard it, but there is no answer to the question: "The soldiers who were still in the prison beat the detainees?"

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer was "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that soldiers made Mr. Kajgana and Mr. Kovacevic to hit one another. Why didn't you mention this in any of your statements when you referred to that incident?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many such incidents. If I could remember them all, I would be very happy if I could repeat them word for word all that happened, but I cannot remember it all. I simply don't recall it when I make my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But in all your statements you described that event, however, without mentioning that particular detail.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I may have recalled those details at that particular moment, because there were so many such details.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you were in solitary confinement. When were you released from it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was then, around the 25th, maybe 26th of April, because at that time I didn't know when it was daytime and when it was night-time, because at night they provoked us and beat us and by day we slept from fear and exhaustion; and sitting, we slept sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified that you saw only one incident when a soldier kicked a detainee in the face, and now you speak about harassment and beatings at night. Now, what is --

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are three cells, three solitary cells. In my cell there are 15, in the first one likewise, and in the third around 12. So perhaps our cell was spared for some reason, but they were taking men out from other cells. One could hear everything, because there is a net above the door, so you can hear everything as if it were in the same room, and that is why I say now that they beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you did not say that yesterday. Why?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That question was not asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday my learned friend specifically asked you about beatings that you had seen or heard. Why didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment. Just one moment. That's a very Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. broad question, Mr. Vasic. Are you able to point to it in the transcript? I recall no such general question. There was certainly a series of questions and very properly limited to particular circumstances. I'm quite happy to be proved wrong, but I have no recollection of any such general question to which this would have been an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I shall try to locate it in the transcript. My learned friend asked about beatings which had taken place in the isolation cells, and the witness said that he remembers how -- that he remembered how a soldier kicked at a detainee in the face who had refused to look at the torch. But I withdraw my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I repeat: I'm happy to be proven wrong, but I have no recollection of it. That's why I thought it proper to raise. It would have been an unlikely question, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I, may I say something, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's asking me very extensively and exhaustively, and I simply remember more questions because I'd like to ask that there be less questions because I experienced it all, and I don't really want to start wondering in my mind here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, sir, we all understand it's a very difficult experience you have to go through here. Unfortunately, it is a necessary one. I'm sure you were forewarned that there would be an unhappy experience for you. Everybody, including counsel for the Defence, recognise that and, I believe, are not trying in any way to make it worse for you; they are only doing their job. But we do understand your difficulties. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us if the persons who took you out of the solitary cell were in military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Persons who took me and my other colleagues out did not have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you were asked by my learned friend a question, and you answered and said that you were interrogated twice during your detention in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was brought there and on the 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you interrogated by an investigator on the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the Public Security Centre, did you say that the interrogations in KP Dom were conducted by a commission of investigators made of Vladicic, former police employee; Koprivica, chief of the printing shop of the KP Dom; and Starovic, former employee of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that they interrogated me, all three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, what kind of an investigating commission was that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did they ask you during those interviews, those members of the commission?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked me about our unit, who was the commander, who was the deputy, our objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did they use force when interrogating you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, when were you registered by the Red Cross first?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd or 26th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And in the Public Security Station, did you state that the Red Cross came for the first time on the 8th of May, 1992, and that it was then registered?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 8th of May 1992? Somebody came, was it the Red Cross or something, but they made a list of people in three rooms only, but they were going around in the presence of the penitentiary guards, so they did not talk to us at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And did you [as translated] make a list of people who were in your room?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my room, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you said that you heard Mr. Kemal Tulek's voice as they -- as he was being beaten. Could you tell us, which room did those sounds come from?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But would you know which part of the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Room 13, and that was as the crow flies not far, perhaps 9 metres from the administrative building, and I heard his screams and cries of pain from that part in the direction of my room, Room 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you mention to OTP investigators that beatings were taking place in a windowless room in the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw that room so I do not know whether it had windows or whether it didn't have any windows, but any beating that took place there we could hear in Room 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But did somebody tell you about such a windowless room?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there was such a room from inmates, but I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name of Mr. Hazim Fulin?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in my room.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you about that room to the left from the entrance behind the duty room?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher help me to show the witness 6/1, Exhibit 6/1, so that we can see which room did Mr. Fulin refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you see the drawing?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please show us the room which Mr. Fulin referred to where the beatings took place.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind the reception area. I think that this is the reception area, so behind it. Since I've never been there, I don't know the -- how these rooms -- in fact where they were located, but based on what Fulin told me, this is what I concluded, that it was behind the reception area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: For the record, can you please show once again this area so that we can identify it.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right here. Based on what I see, I think that this here is the reception area, and then based on what he told me, I concluded that this took place behind it, behind the reception area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is pointing to the left wing of the administrative building. He is pointing to a room which is second from the right in the direction to the left, and it is labelled with a word "guard."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please show us in which part of the prisoners' building you were located.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in this part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On which floor?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second floor, Room 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the record, the witness indicated to a building number 1, above the room which is labelled as warehouse, and the witness stated that his room was on the second floor of that building. Thank you. We will not be needing this drawing anymore. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether, on the 30th July of 1994, you gave a statement to the investigators of the Security Centre in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday, when asked, I told you that these dates which were important and which took place after I was released, I had trouble remembering these dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever give a statement to the investigators of the Public Security Station?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will read out to you a part of your statement given to the members of the Public Security Station in the document on B/C/S language. You can find this segment on page 5, at the bottom of the page: "On the 25th of June of 1992 --"

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of June, 1992. "From rooms 11 and 12, as well as from my room, a group of 50 people was taken out from the KP Dom, and they never returned and nothing was heard of them. This group included Munib Veiz; Zulfo Veiz; Nail Hodzic; Salem Bico; Kemal Dzelilovic; Altoka, Omer; a man known as Kiselica, a son of Alija; three Rikalo brothers, one of whose names was Husein; Nurko Nisic; Kemal Tulek" - I apologise - "a man called Balic, about 65 years old, and his son, about 20 years old; a certain Krunoslav, journalist, from -- journalist in a Zagreb magazine; Mato, a medical technician in the Foca hospital; and Konjo, Halim." Did you give this statement to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you stated that upon being released from the KP Dom you found out that Mr. Nisic was beaten by a certain Zelenovic. Do you know whether Mr. Zelenovic was a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you stated that when the beatings took place, the list would come in from the administrative building. Did you mean that in fact the guard was bringing in the list from that administrative building?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the guard would bring the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guard would also read the list out, standing at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was the list printed or written -- or handwritten on the paper?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to an incident which took place in the isolation cell and pertained to Mr. Duric, during your stay at the KP Dom did you see somebody beating the inmates?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: During your stay at the KP Dom, did you see somebody hitting inmates with your own eyes, in addition to this incident which took place in the isolation cell while you were staying there with Mr. Duric?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see -- I saw Sulejman Celik being stopped by the guards after the visit of these journalists from a magazine called Duga. I don't remember which guards exactly stopped him, but they did beat him after that. And after he was beaten, he came to my room, with visible bruises. So I asked him personally, "What happened?" And he said, "They beat me for talking to the journalists from Duga."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you state to the OTP investigators that on 17 September of 1992 a group of inmates was taken to pick plums and that they never came back, just -- they never came back and neither did the two guards that went with them?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of what happened to these inmates and the guards that didn't come back?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you stated that you knew that a body of Konjo Halim's brother was found. Do you know where his body was found?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from his father that it was found at Previla in a stream.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the settlement Previla is located with respect to Foca?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the north, along the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you stated that on the 5th of May, 1993, Dr. Ibro Karovic was taken out of the KP Dom. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Dr. Ibro Karovic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found him on the 23rd of October in 1993 in KP Dom. I found him in Kula, in a camp called Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you stated that on the 12th of October of 1992, your relative was exchanged, taken away for exchange in KP Dom. Can you give us his name, please?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My nephew was taken away on the 20th of September of 1992. This is true hundred per cent, and his name is Nermin Hadzimusic. I never found out what happened to him. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you mention this in your previous statements?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you gave precise dates of exchanges and people that were exchanged. Why didn't you give these exact dates and names in your previous statements to the OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did, but I don't know, because I do remember these dates very well, and I will always keep this in my memory and repeat it if needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You discussed exchanges, but you did not state all of the dates that you had given us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am more precise now because I think that this is the main hearing, and it is important for me to give exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you also mentioned for the first time the journalist that visited KP Dom. Why hadn't you mentioned this before, either to the OTP investigators or to the workers of the Public Security Centre?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just recently said that there were a lot of these events, and if I were to discuss all of these events that I remember, there would be no end to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So is it for the same reason that you did not bring up before how you found out about a conversation between Mr. Krnojelac and Mr. Cankusic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So does it mean that you remember this more vividly now than in 1994 when you gave the first statement, in 1996 when you gave the second, and in 1999 when you gave the third statement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I definitely remember better now than in 1994 because I was -- when I was released, I was in a really difficult situation, both physically and mentally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So can you explain why you did not bring this up with the OTP investigators about this conversation between Mr. Krnojelac and Mr. Cankusic, and it's very important to this case in which Mr. Krnojelac stands accused? Did the investigator ask you whether you knew of the discussions that Mr. Krnojelac had with various persons?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember this well now. I think that I was asked that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you stated that you listened to the conversation in front of the window of Room 12, a conversation between Mr. Cankusic and another individual, in which Mr. Cankusic stated that he went to the warden to inquire about his sons. Can you clarify whether you heard this directly from Mr. Cankusic, or you found this out by listening to the conversation that I just described?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain. In my Room 13, there was Dervis Cankusic, a relative of Cankusic. He talked to him, and at the time I passed by and I heard something, and then Dervis later on explained it to me properly, so this is how I know about this whole story. So this whole conversation was related to me by Dervis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In which room was Mr. Cankusic Dervis staying?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my room, number 13, and also in my room, number 3, because the Room 13 contained, in fact, four separate rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, you stated that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please wait for the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you stated that Mr. Cankusic was talking to Dervis, to Mr. Dervis about the details of his visit to Mr. Krnojelac. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I understood it correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, did I understand you, that in fact this is how it took place, this is how it occurred? Who was Mr. Cankusic talking to through the window?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were coming back from either lunch or dinner, I don't remember now, there were the stairs and a path leading to the entrance of this building where Rooms 12 and 13 were. So there's a path leading to it, and Cankusic Dervis was at the head of this column so he could talk to this relative of his through the window, and the rest of us approached him, and then all of us together entered the building, the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So by which window was the relative of Mr. Dervis standing by?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Room 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, whether these conversations which were taking place across the window frame were allowed in KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you coming back from your meal escorted by guards?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, how did the guard permit such a conversation to take place?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guard never walked close to us. He would normally stay at least 5 metres behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you in your statement given to the Public Security Station in Sarajevo, did you state there that the situation in KP Dom improved after the Red Cross from England visited KP Dom sometime in mid-June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, during your stay at the Kula camp, did you talk to your brother Ismet and your family? Did you have a telephone conversation with them?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by telephone, but I talked to them from a car via walkie-talkies or something called like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you stated that prior to your arrival in KP Dom you did not know Mr. Krnojelac. Did you, in your second statement to the OTP investigators, state something else, in fact, that you knew him as a math teacher?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never knew him, but I learned that he was a math teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just one more question. During your replies given to questions put by my learned friend, you frequently used the term "Chetniks." This expression, "Chetniks," is it synonymous with Serbs or do you have in mind members of a special military unit?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means nothing to me. I heard from the Serbs in KP Dom, because there were some Serb detainees there, I heard them refer to themselves as Chetniks, so this is where I got this expression. But I don't call them any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was that the first time you heard that expression?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From them, yes, but I also heard this expression used before from the previous war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now, did these people that referred to themselves as Chetnik, were they members of the military formations, military units?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Defence has no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Kuo, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for giving evidence. You may now leave. You may take your time, if you have any difficulty, but you are now finished and your experience is over. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, the next witness has protective measures, so the screens will have to be erected. But you have some documents, I understand, that you want to tender, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The screens can be erected whilst that is going on. It won't disturb us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday Ms. Manas showed us a drawing that she had in her booklet, and we have meanwhile submitted this drawing -- a copy of this drawing, a big one, to the registrar, and we would like to tender it into evidence, maybe as an exhibit related to her report. That would be Prosecution Exhibit 41, and we may call it 41/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is this a reproduction or an enlargement of the one that was in her book?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's an enlargement. It was a very small book and a very small drawing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you any objection to that, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be Exhibit P41/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the other documents the Prosecution would like to tender into evidence are related to the Witness 96. According to an agreement with Defence counsel, we would like to enter the transcript of this witness into evidence, and also her exit permit to leave Foca. And in the trial binders it is -- the transcript has the ID number 186, and the permit has the numbers 185 and 185A. However, the example of the transcript in the trial binder is not the one that you will receive or have received already, because we have blacked certain parts in this transcript that will not be tendered into evidence, according to the agreement with Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean the document that has just been handed in is a redacted form of the transcript that was in our binders?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour,.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. That will be Exhibit P186. Now, are the exit permits similarly redacted?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. The exit permits are not redacted. They should come into this trial under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then those two documents will be Exhibit P185 and P185A, and they will be under seal. Perhaps I just should get this checked. There is going to be no cross-examination of Witness 96?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, have you got any other documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's related, actually, to the witness who is now testifying. We have, of course, again a sheet, a witness sheet with a pseudonym and birthday and some other names on it, and it has also to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it would be a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be -- have you got it there? That will be Exhibit P415 and it will be under seal. I've assumed your consent, Mr. Bakrac, perhaps wrongly, but you've consented to each of these so far, these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. You mean this last document having to do with the protected witness or the transcript? Yes, yes, we do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. P415. It will be under seal. Yes, the blinds will be lowered whilst the witness is brought into Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Will you please make the solemn declaration in the document being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Your witness, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have a sheet of paper in front of you, and the first name of this sheet of paper, is that your name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the date below, is that your birth date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on this same sheet of paper you find four other names. If you want to refer to these people listed on the sheet of paper, please do not use the name, but rather the number.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you help him with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I forgot to greet you, sorry.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say Bosniak, do you mean a Muslim, Muslim?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you married when the war started?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you have children?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes, two; a daughter and a younger son.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where did you live before the war, in which neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: In Foca, Donje Polje neighbourhood community.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you live in a private house or an apartment building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: In a private house.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you own this house, or was it your family house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: It was a house. I inherited it, so, yes, it was my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is this house still standing, do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What happened to the house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Serbs put fire to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: It happened in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you actually see it happen? Did you see it burn?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I did, yes. I was in the town in a residential building, and from there I could see buildings all around Donje Polje burn.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said that Serbs set fire on it. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I know it because they had taken the whole of the town of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was your profession before and during the war -- sorry, what was your profession before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I was employed in the KP Dom, or rather, I was a guard in the penitentiary in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which time period did you work there as a guard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: From (redacted) until April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was the capacity of the prison? How many prisoners were there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: The capacity was up to 1.000, perhaps 1100 or 1200, but when the aggression began, there were about 500 or 600 inmates in the KP Dom compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say 1.000, up to 1.200, does this include the entire KP Dom complex including outposts, or the centre, just this prison -- main prison building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: The outside buildings, no. Well, we had some working sites, workshops outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The KP Dom itself, the main facility, was it a male prison?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes, a male prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What about the female convicts, were they housed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Women were kept at Velecevo prison, and it is a locality 2.5 kilometres away from Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was this facility for females? Was it under the command of the main KP Dom, the male KP Dom, or was it independent?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes, it was under the control of the male part of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there a prison farm as an outpost of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, there wasn't a farm only. There was also a building unit, a metal-working unit, timber industry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's go one after the other. The prison farm, where was it, and how many prisoners did work there during peacetime?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: That farm was 3 kilometres away from Foca, and there was some livestock breeding there, then there was also the livestock farm, the pig breeding farm, cattle breeding, and also poultry farm. The number of convicts was around 80 to 90 to 100.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they also sleep there? Were they housed in this farm complex?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is where they slept.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was there a fish pond, and if so, where was it and how many prisoners worked there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes, there was a fish hatchery, a fish pond. If I remember well, it was in 1989. I can't really remember when it was opened, but it was at a distance of some 15, 16 kilometres. And convicts were also kept there; that is, they lived there and worked there and slept there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many convicts worked on this fish farm?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a particularly large -- or rather, the capacity was large, but there were about 25 men, 20. It varied.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a construction firm. Where was this, and what was it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: The construction unit had one plant in Foca and another one in Sarajevo. And that in Sarajevo, we built residential buildings, and in Foca likewise, that is, the convicts were engaged in building residential or houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did convicts also work in the Miljevina mine?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes. We also had that, and we had that particular work site. Miljevina is at a distance of some 12 kilometres from Foca. We had a contract with the Miljevina mine, and we used to send about 30 to 40 convicts to work there. And again, it varied on the needs of the mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when the convicts worked in the mine or at all these other places, were they paid for their work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes, every convict was remunerated for the work he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they all get the same salary, or did that depend on the work they did or their qualification?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: No, no qualifications. It depended on the nature of work, his performance as a worker, the length of time, the kind of work. For instance, those who were construction workers before the war, they would get some 200 marks, but those were exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And those who worked in the mine, did they get the same salary as, for instance, those working at the fish pond, or was there is a difference?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: No. There was a difference because it is harder to work as a miner than at a fish farm. Also, they wanted, of course, to be assigned to jobs where they could make more money.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall what the salary was of those people who worked in the mine?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I don't know because I never worked there. Only I know from the stories I heard that they were remunerated quite well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you worked in the KP Dom as a guard. Were you under the supervision of the police or Ministry of Justice or the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: No. We were under the Ministry of Justice of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In April 1992, who was the warden of the prison?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Before the aggression, the warden was Radojica Tesevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know what profession Mr. Tesevic actually learned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I think he graduated in sociology in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was Mr. Tesevic involved in politics, do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes. He was in all the authorities in Foca. He was the president of the executive board. I also think he was the president of the former central committee. I'm not sure, but I know that he was the mayor of the municipality and also the head of government of the municipal government, and he used to be a teacher and to teach at the teacher's school in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you mentioned the central committee, does that mean the communist party? To which party do you refer?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he a member of any of the new formed parties? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: No, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Having -- to become the warden of the KP Dom, would you need to be involved in politics? His position -- Mr. Tesevic's position in the KP Dom, does it have to do -- does it have anything to do with all of these functions you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What were the duties and responsibilities of Mr. Tesevic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: He was the prison warden, and all the work sites and all the business units were all under him; that is, he was in charge of everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was his deputy before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Hasan Klapuh, and after that Alija Berberkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What were the duties of Mr. Klapuh and Mr. Berberkic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, the same kind of duties. What they usually did was to take care of security and then acted as wardens when Radojica Tesevic would be away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And to take care of security, what does it mean, actually? In practical terms, what did they do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: They took care of security, the guard duty, headed disciplinary commissions for the convicts, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was the chief of the guards before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Before the war it was Mitar Rasevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the commander of the guards, besides being the commander of the guards, did he have any other duties?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, he was in charge of disciplinary procedure in case of some guard -- transgressions by guards, and he also visited persons kept in solitary confinement. I mean, he was only responsible for security or, rather, for the guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many guards worked in the KP Dom on an average?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: On the average, about a hundred, but it depended on the number of work places and whether there were any vacancies or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the guards work in shift, and if so, how were the shifts organised?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes, the guards worked in shifts, and there were also some guard posts with only one shift. That is, for a while it was between 8.00 and 4.00, from 4.00 to 12.00, and from 12.00, that is, from midnight until 8.00. And later on we changed the working hours and worked -- and would work for two days. The first shift, that is, from 6.00 till 3.00; for two days from 3.00 p.m. to 2200; and the third shift would be -- we would do for two days from 2200 till 6.00 in the morning, and then we would get two days off.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, was he involved in politics? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: No, as far as I know, except that he was a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Savo Todovic work in the KP Dom before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes. Savo Todovic too was a clerk in the KP Dom or, rather, he started as a guard, but then he graduated from the vocational administrative school and then became a clerk in charge of the registry of convicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As the clerk for the registry of convicts, what did he have to do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, a clerk in charge of convicts, well, it depends. There is a clerk who is responsible for sports activities; and there is another person who is responsible for the employment of convicts; and there was also a man who was responsible for criminal investigation techniques; and there was also another employee, another clerk, who was a photographer, who took photographs of the convicts upon their arrival in the penitentiary.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Todovic do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Mr. Todovic was responsible for the employment of convicts and he was also involved in the criminal analysis or, rather, files of the convicts. He was the one who kept the files of convicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he involved in politics? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: As far as I know, before the war he was a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Speaking of the chain of command in the KP Dom before the war, who belonged actually to the prison management? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Specifically, in the prison administration, well, everybody belonged. The guards, number one; two, rehabilitating officers; and then the legal department, accountants, the business unit, health service, the construction unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who were the chiefs of the units related to economic matters? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, let me start from the beginning. Radojica Tesevic was the warden of the penitentiary, Hasan Klapuh, then succeeded by Alija Berberkic, then the head of the rehabilitation service. The chief of guards was Mitar Rasevic. The business unit, Drina, it was Mujo Smajkan, and that business unit was then divided into the farm, construction unit, agriculture, fish hatchery.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The business -- you said the business unit Drina. Does that include all these economical parts or is that something else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: No. It covered -- it embraced all the business parts and it was called Drina Business Unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mujo -- I just have this "Mujo." I didn't understand the last name. Did he have a specific title within the structure? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, we wouldn't call it title. We said manager of the Drina Business Unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know if this Drina Business Unit made profits?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what was done with this profit? Did it remain in the prison or was it referred to the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: As for the profit, it was distributed between the convict and civilian person, guards, and Ministry of Justice, and of course for production materials, for the purchase of livestock or fishstock, timber industry, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say it was distributed also to the convicts, you mean the salaries, or was there something additional, in addition?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: There was the remuneration for convicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let us now talk about the reporting structure that was in place before the war. To whom did you report and how did you do it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I reported to the head of my department who was actually the commander of guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how did you do that, verbally or did you write reports?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, it depended. Sometimes I did it in writing and sometimes verbally.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you did it in writing, did you have a report book, or was it single sheets? What actually was it? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, each position had a book of -- an official book of reports, a log-in book, and this book was transferred between employees when they were taking over their duties. And if there was a problem that needed to be reported, then that would be done in writing, and this report would be delivered to the chief of guards, commander of guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This book that you mentioned, did each section have such a book, that is, the guard, the tutors, and the other sections?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, each position had this kind of logbook book, and all new moments, all new facts that pertained to that position, would be written into that book. And the heads of various units would give both verbal and written reports to their chiefs, and those who were on duty in the shift had to give written, typed reports that would go to the chief of guards, to the chief of rehabilitation unit, and to the warden. And all changes would be entered into that report, all changes that took place during that particular shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like you to explain to the Court this reporting system in relation to unusual events. For instance, in case of a suicide during your shift, what would you have to do, and what would happen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, this is how it would be: If this were to take place during my shift, then I would inform the officer on duty, and then he in turn would inform the warden of the prison part, and then the warden -- the chief of the rehabilitation service. The warden would call in the police. The police would come in and investigate and interrogate the person on duty who had to be present during the -- during this investigation, and there would also be an investigative judge who would be involved in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And why would the officer on duty inform the warden in such a case?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes, that was his duty, to inform everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you actually ever experience such an incident while you were working in the KP Dom, a suicide?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes, it did take place. We had a person who hanged himself in the furniture factory. I was making a round of the factory, and as I was making my round I noticed a person who was hanging in the upholstery department. I informed the others through my walkie-talkie, Motorola, and then other guards came in and secured this site until the people who were in charge came to the site as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on this occasion, did the warden also come and take action?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Definitely. That was his duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In case of -- another example, in case of a violent act between, let's say, prisoners, or in relation to a guard to a prisoner, or the other way around, what would happen? What would you do in such a case?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, we had those kind of incidents. There were cases where inmates would fight amongst themselves, and in that case we would intervene and separate the inmates. We would get them to give a written statement and then they would be locked in the isolation cells. At the end of my shift I would normally write a written report to the chief of guards, and he in turn would send this report to the chief of the rehabilitation unit, and he in turn would send it to the warden of -- prison warden. After that there would be a disciplinary procedure. There would be a commission who would decide on disciplinary measures which would be implemented in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In case a prisoner would have a complaint, let's say a complaint about the guards, what was in place for such a complaint? What would he have to do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: As far as disciplinary measures were concerned, or at least a complaint lodged against a guard, an inmate would have to write a written report and then turn it over to his rehabilitation officer; and the rehabilitation officer would go up the chain all the way to the chief of rehabilitation unit; and he in turn would decide whether this complaint should be forwarded to Mitar Rasevic, the chief of guards, or to the warden. If guards were to overstep their authorities, then there would be a disciplinary measure. It depends on what kind of an infringement it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in case a prisoner wanted to see the warden, what would he have to do to get there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: In order for him to get to the warden, he would have to apply to us first, and then we in turn would inform the chief of guards of this request, and he in turn would inform the chief of rehabilitation unit. If this was some kind of a lesser-degree incident, then this would go through the rehabilitation officer and then on to the head of the rehabilitation unit. And there were certain dates when the warden would see people who had certain complaints, but there were also -- there was a possibility where he could see people who had complaints outside of those specific predetermined dates or hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you said he would have to apply to you, the guards, first, does that mean he would hand over a written request or could they ask to see the warden verbally? Was there a formal way to do it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: We would collect reports in rooms every evening, and we had a book, or rather it was a sheet of paper, where we would enter the number of convicts in the rooms, which room this pertained to, and we would also write specifics concerning medical status or other things that were entered into the report. And then in turn this would be entered into the log-in book when the other guard would come to take over, and these convicts in the morning would then be taken for an audience with officials.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Which disciplinary measures did the warden have at his disposal in case a guard mistreated a prisoner? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, this depended on a measure. If this was a simple case of overstepping authorities, then this guard would go to a disciplinary commission. He would be suspended, and the disciplinary commission would then issue a disciplinary measure. Usually, that was in the form of a monetary fee that had to be paid.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In a more serious incident?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, if this was serious, then dismissal would ensue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how would the warden get involved in this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, I'll repeat it once again. Depends on the gravity of the incident. If it was a disciplinary sanction that ensued, then the guard had a right to appeal in a certain time frame, but if there were no appeals, either from the guard or from the warden, then it would stand. And if there was an appeal, then the disciplinary commission would sit again and then decide in a new proceeding. If this was a grave -- an incident of a grave nature, then that person would be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that the involvement of the warden depends on the gravity of the incident. Could you give us examples for serious incidents that would actually involve the warden at any, at any case?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: You mean if it pertained to the guards?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, we had cases where the guards would go outside with their weapons and shoot in various celebrations, during holidays. We also had a case where a guard borrowed his uniform to a murderer, and as a result of that, he was automatically dismissed in an urgent procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there ever a case where a guard beat up a detainee or a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, there were cases of that as well, but very few.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And would the warden get involved in this? Would he be informed through all this various chain of command steps?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Naturally, because the warden also had to report to the Ministry of Justice. He had to report to them annually on the occasions in which a baton was used, and then the Ministry of Justice would review the case and decide whether the use of baton was justified.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did the war break out in Foca, the initial shooting, let's say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, really, this is what we have been talking about. Is there any dispute about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just lead him, just lead him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, were you still in the prison?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many prisoners were in the prison at that time; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, approximately 400. Well, this was long time ago for me to remember with precision, but I remember that on Monday at 3.30, certain inmates escaped through the wall because they felt in the air that something was coming, and they arranged this escape. Approximately 60 or 70 of them escaped between the gates or guard booths number six and five at the gate number three. Between the gates there were the booths for the guard. And they called the officer on duty, informed him of this escape. The guard then informed the warden to get instructions on whether they should shoot or not. The warden said, "Do not shoot. Let them run."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you present on this day when this happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes, I was present there. I was working. I was a guard on duty, and they fled past me. And the warden was in the compound, and so was the chief of the rehabilitation unit. They had a conversation which I am not familiar with. And the inmates escaped through the wall that was by the gate, and then we organised ourselves and we started basically catching them and bringing them back to the KP Dom. Some of them managed to escape. They were fleeing in various directions. Some of them went across the bridge, some went through the river, and some of them fled to the forest because the forest was maybe 50 or 100 metres away from the wall.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And when was your last working day at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: My last working day was, I believe, Friday or Saturday. I don't recall. I think that on Wednesday at 9.30, the shooting began. We were in the -- we spread ourselves between the administrative building and a guard's booth. I was there during that day, and then my mother and my late wife called me asking me to come back home. They were afraid; they were crying. I left my pistol, I left my rifle, and I went home. And I never went back to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These few days that you spent in the KP Dom after the shooting actually had started and before you left, were the guards still there? Was still the -- did the prison still function?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, the prison was partially still functioning. The guards remained there due to other inmates that were still in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what kind of weapons did you have at that time, the guards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: The guards had semi-automatic weapons, Kalashnikovs, and pistols, and the latest machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in addition to the weapons that you and the guards actually had with you, were they weapons stored in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes. We had a room where the weapons and ammunition were kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you receive orders from the warden or your direct superior what to do with these weapons, weapon? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I think that I was accidentally there when the phone rang at one occasion. I picked up the receiver and I heard the voice of Mr. Radojica Tesevic, and he ordered to break into this room where the weapons were held, to take out the locks from the weapons and to throw them into the storage or utility room, and that was done exactly so. All of these locks from semi-automatic and automatic weapons were put in a sack and it was taken to the utility heating room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And why -- do you know why you had to do that, what was behind that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't know. I didn't understand why that had to be done, but it was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you left the KP Dom and you left your weapon behind. Did you have a private weapon at home?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you did not return afterwards to the KP Dom. Are you aware if the Muslim side took over the KP Dom at some point in time? Would you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, the Muslim side, I think, held the KP Dom for some three or four days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you know if they detained Serbs in the KP Dom at that time? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, because at the time I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with the remaining prisoners when you left? Were they moved somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes. Later on when I was exchanged and I came to Sarajevo, I met an inmate who was there during the whole time, and he told me that they were loaded onto trucks that transported furniture and they were taken to Spuz, which was a prison in Titograd. Since Titograd would not have them, some of them were taken through Bosnia, and some through Serbia, back to Bosnia, and some were around Tuzla. They were turned over and put into the KP Dom or, rather, prison in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "they," do you mean all remaining detainees of all ethnicities, or who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: They were mostly Muslims - perhaps a few Croats, but mostly Muslims - because Serbs were released, freed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that, that Serbs were released?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: This inmate told me so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While you were in Foca, still in Foca in April 1992, did you ever come across convicts that were walking freely around?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I didn't, because I really didn't move around a lot in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: After you left the KP Dom, where did you go? Did you actually stay in your house or did you go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I stayed at home and I was there for about two days. I immediately noticed there was no one around but that there was still gunfire.
