utterances.text: Yes, the entrance into the compound. And the administration building was to the left and to the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned this particular room with the rings -- with the metallic rings on the floor. Was that a room -- for what was this room used during the peacetime when you worked there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, during the peacetime it was used in those instances where convicts, when they were drunk, would be locked in that room until they sobered up; and once they sobered up, we would take them back into the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the sound of shots in relation to beatings?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes, in the evening, in the evening hours --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How often did you hear --

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: -- in front of the building. Well, in the beginning it was more frequent; it took place more frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever hear -- could you ever connect the shots to beatings, or was it just shots? Like, could it be some --

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Those were just shots. I know that those who worked in the metal workshop, they said that they washed the car belonging to Kedi, Zastava vehicle, that we used to use to drive -- to transport fish in it. They told us that they washed the blood from the car.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you hear car noises after the beatings that you described?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, it's a typical sound produced by this type of Zastava car, and this came as a result of the exhaust pipe being damaged. So they used it to transport the dead bodies and then the car would come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you hear the car?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: This invariably took place in the evening, in May, June, July, and August.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever find out who beat the victims? Could you hear it from the sounds or did the victims later tell you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: No. I personally didn't hear it, but I heard from other inmates that the KP guards beat them. And on one occasion I saw Predrag Stefanovic, after the meal, I saw him slap Pace Pasanovic, known as Pace. I saw him slap him twice. And everything else took place either in that passing room or by the gate. Sometimes they also beat people in the isolation cells.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You just mentioned this incident with guard -- Mr. Stefanovic slapping Pace. When did this take place and where were you and what did you see?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I was in Room 20 and waited for lunch, and we were observing them as they were leaving the dining-room and lining up. So he, in front of the kitchen, approached Pace and slapped him twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is incident 5.10 in the indictment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you recall when it was approximately, which month?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, I already told you: All of this happened in June, July, August, September. I really cannot remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever see detainees being beaten by soldiers within the compound?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes. It took place one day around 1, 1.30, Room 16 went out to eat lunch. And they finished their lunch and they started coming out and lining up, and at that moment a group of six to eight armed soldiers entered the compound of KP Dom. They approached and I saw from Room 18, or rather, Room 20, I saw as they slapped Witness 214 and they cursed his balija God, told him, "You balija, put your head down and put your hands behind your back." And when Room 16 finished their lunch, they interrupted serving lunch to everybody else until Serbs from the compound finished their lunch and went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness was referring to the incident 5.12 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned that the soldiers were armed. Was that according to the rules in the prison, that soldiers with arms could go there and enter the compound with arms?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Nobody was ever allowed to come into the compound armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you referring to the system you knew from your work; is that what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when this incident happened, were guards present?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Only Milenko Cancar was present, and he interrupted lunch. I saw that he became red. He stopped eating and sent those people back to Room 16 and did not let them come out until these soldiers left.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you discussed with us several people who were taken out and disappeared and that who were beaten. Did you fear to be taken out and disappear as well when you saw that happen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, I naturally was afraid and, however, since I had worked there previously and since I knew that I could not be blamed for anything and since I knew the people around, I did not have terrible fear. However, it was weird, it was strange, especially when they beat people and we could hear moans and screams, and we would go into another room where we could not hear those screams. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These victims, do they have anything in common that made them a target for such violence? Could you, could you see something or could you figure out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I really could not figure out why those people were imprisoned. There were over 530 people, and I could not really deduce why they were locked up because if they were guilty, they would have run away. But they remained there and they really didn't know why they were locked up, but their reasoning was, "Why escape if we are not guilty."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I was asking you about these people who were selected for beatings and disappeared. Did they have something in common, that they became a target of this special mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: No, nothing in common.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know a detainee Rasim Jusufovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Rasim Jusufovic was an educator, a teacher. He worked in an elementary school Veselin Maslesa, and he was a physical education teacher. His wife was a Serb. He had two children, a son and a daughter. When all of this started, he fled to Montenegro because his wife was originally from there. After that, he went to Voyvodina, and supposedly his wife called the school to inquire as to whether he could go back to work. They replied yes, and they went to the border at -- to the border at which place Rasim was arrested and he was brought into the KP Dom into Room 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So does it mean he told that -- he himself gave you this information, or how do you come to know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: He told all that himself, how he had fled and how he had come back to Foca, because we shared the room, or rather, we shared even the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he have conversations, conversations with the -- with Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krnojelac was Rasim's colleague, and one morning the guards called him and took him to gate 1. He was absent for about half an hour, an hour, I don't know exactly, and he talked to Mr. Krnojelac, and he came back to the room. I knew that they were colleagues, that they were friends, so nothing bad about it. And Rasim then told me that we would be divided into four groups, that one group would be court-martialed, that another group would be taken to the free territory, that a third group would be exchanged, and that a fourth group would stay behind in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did this conversation take place, the conversation between Mr. Krnojelac and Rasim?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: It was sometime in June or July, I cannot remember the date. But I know it, and I'm quite positive about what I'm saying now because Rasim told me about that. I know how he went and how he came back. And when I asked him, "Who told you all that?" He said, "Krnojelac told me." And that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You say "and that's how it was." In which group were you, could you figure out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I was in the group because I stayed until 1994, so I was with that group.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this group that you mentioned, the first group that was to be court-martialed, what happened to this group? Could you figure out who was in this group and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Those who were taken in the afternoon between half past three and 7.00 in the evening, they were allegedly taken before a judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever see a judge in the KP Dom, or did you see a court-martial functioning in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I only saw Slavisa Prodanovic in the KP Dom because I know that he was a judge before the war, but I don't think really -- I don't know -- no, he was not in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you mentioned the group that was to be exchanged. Were people exchanged, and did they actually later show -- were released?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, say in August, I remember Vlatko Pljevaljcic came in to Room 16 and asked for volunteers, and one -- I was one of those volunteers. And he said to me, "You, come out. You are not going." And he was followed by Predrag Stefanovic who came in, and a line was formed. But then Predrag, he went out and came back with a list and then started calling out names from that list. Those men left through gate 1 and did not come back. That was August, September, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know who was in this group? Could you name anyone?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, for instance, I remember Crneta because he was next to me in the line. I don't really remember many because as soon as they had formed the line and took me away from it, I went to the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this Crneta, what is his name, what is his full name, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: His last name was Crneta. He was a manager of a unit in Maglic, but his name, his first name, no, I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall that a detainee once escaped?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I remember that very well. That was detainee number 216. A group of 25 Muslims was working in the metal workshop - that was a metal shop making frames for kiosks - and also a car mechanic shop, and they also maintained the boiler room. This witness fled from the compound across the bridge, reached the town, and from the town through Ustikolina he reached Gornje Polje, from there he got to Zastava which is above Foca, and he headed for Scepan Polje. And allegedly, as he says, fog fell, so he lost his way and ended up in a village, and villagers captured him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As a consequence of this escape, did you suffer anything?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, we -- the others, yes, they suffered the consequences because our rations were cut down by 75 per cent, all of us. And those who worked with him, they indeed suffered consequences. They were beaten, battered, locked up in solitary confinement. Todovic threatened, threatened with a pistol that he would kill them all if he were not captured.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What happened when this detainee was brought back? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, we were not aware that he had been caught. One day they came around ten or 11, took us out into the yard of the compound in front of the kitchen next to a walnut tree, lined us up, and all of a sudden Zekovic turned up with Savo Todovic and Mr. Krnojelac. Mr. Krnojelac was wearing a uniform, and Savo Todovic was wearing a military uniform, too, that is, of the former JNA. And Savo Todovic then took us to task, or rather, delivered a lecture telling us how the Serbs were humane and good, and how they could have killed him but did not want to, and along those lines. Then they took us back to the room, and they [as translated] were locked up in the isolation cell, and he spent a month there. But we felt that, as I have said, through the rations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Krnojelac on other occasions in the, in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I used to see him every day when he'd come to have his lunch -- or rather, breakfast in the morning when he would go there to have his meal, because all the KP Dom employees had their breakfast and lunch and dinner in the compound as the restaurant outside the compound was not really in proper order, it could not -- was not usable because it had been devastated, destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say you saw him every day, was that throughout your detention or only through a period?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, I'd see him -- I saw him when I went to the window. When I would be too tired of lying down or walking up and down, then I would go to the window, and he came to have his breakfast around ten or half past ten and wearing a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when was the -- was the restaurant outside the KP Dom reestablished at a point in time during your detention?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, I think it was -- that it went back into operation in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you continue --

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Late 1993 -- no, I don't remember. But yes, yes, it -- yes, it opened again, and they did not come again. It was only Mitar Rasevic and Savo Todovic who continued coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me clarify that. When the restaurant was operating, did you continue to see Mr. Krnojelac going to the meals as you described before, or did it stop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: No, no, no. He stopped coming to the kitchen in the compound because they all began then to patronise the restaurant after it was reopened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you saw Mr. Krnojelac, was he alone, or was he accompanied by other prison staff or even people from outside?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: At times alone, at times with other staff, with Mitar or Savo, and on one occasion he was also with some commission of the Ministry of Justice from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you actually see this commission and Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: In the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Touring around, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I recognised one of them because he was a local from Foca who used to work for us as a rehabilitator and then moved over to Kula in Sarajevo. The others I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who was this person? What was the name of this person you knew?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Cvorcan [Realtime transcript read in error "Sveten"] was his last name. I don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how do you know it was a commission of the Ministry of Justice? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript says "Sreten," and I think it is a misprint. I do not think that is the correct name. The witness did not say that. Cvorcan, and the witness said he did not know the first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you maybe spell -- to clarify this, could you spell the name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: C-v-o-r-c-a-n. He held some office or other. He came from Butmir prison in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you said it was a commission of the Ministry of Justice. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: From guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was the accused replaced and by whom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac was replaced in 1993, I don't remember the date, and Sekulovic I think, Ranko or - what was it? What was his name - came to succeed him. He used to work for the promotion and public relations department at Oslobodenje in Slatina which is about 12 kilometres from Foca. He came to replace Mr. Krnojelac. That was allegedly a change between the civilian and military authority. But only he was replaced, and Savo Todovic and Rasevic stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that was allegedly a change between the civilian and military authorities. What do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I meant that as soon as the International Red Cross arrived, changes for the better began to happen in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But just let me repeat what is in the transcript. You said -- the replacement time: "That was allegedly a change between the civilian and the military authorities." What do you refer to when you say that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: The civilian authorities exceeded the military authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Because the International Red Cross had entered the prison. The military authorities would not allow - why, I do not know - would not allow the Red Cross to enter the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that's still not an answer to your question, and it is rather an important issue. What you want to obtain from the witness is how he was able to distinguish between those who were military authorities and those who were civilian authorities. That's what you're really after, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you heard the Presiding Judge. Could you answer this? How do you distinguish between the two, the civilian and the military Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authorities?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac was replaced and Sekulovic came instead. And as soon as Sekulovic arrived, the Red Cross also entered the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You had explained to us in the beginning of your testimony or, rather, in the beginning, the normal structure that you knew from the KP Dom when you worked there, and then you mentioned announcements, that you heard that Mr. Krnojelac became the warden. Do you say that it was the military authorities ruling the prison when Mr. Krnojelac was the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: The party assigned people in all institutions. If you were not a member of the SDS, then you could not become an executive.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From which facts do you come to say that it was the military authorities that were in charge in the prison before the Red Cross came? From which facts do you have this opinion?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Because they were all in JNA uniforms, so I concluded that by the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What uniforms did the guards wear?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: The guards were in their old uniforms, and then they changed into multicoloured police uniforms, because they spent 15 days in the prison and 15 days on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, I simply stopped seeing them in the KP Dom, because -- and then a shift would change and he would be back in the KP Dom for 10 or 15 days and would then go to the front line again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, who was second in command under the accused Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I don't think there was anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And then Mr. Rasevic, when you look at the prison hierarchy, where was he? Where was he placed then?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. This is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, it's not. It's not a leading question. It's a simple question: Where did he fit into the prison hierarchy? There is evidence that he did fit within it. The question is where. I think you're drawing an inference from the fact that they had been previously discussing the second in command, but it's not asking whether he was second in command; it's just asking where he was. That's not a leading question. You proceed, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please answer the question, Witness. Where was Mr. Rasevic in this chain of command in the prison? During your detention, not before. During your detention, where was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Mitar Rasevic was the commander of the police or, rather, of the prison guards. And Savo Todovic was a kind of a responsible clerk, because he had either graduated from a higher administrative school or a legal school, and he was a clerk responsible for us, because he assigned various jobs and tasks to us. That is, "You go to the factory, to the farm, to Maglic, to Tjentiste, to the mine," because it was a warden's duty to do that thing and to assign people to various jobs. It was always the responsibility of a clerk in charge of such matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic and Mr. Todovic, did they have the same level of authority within the chain of command or was one the superior of the other?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. They were all subordinated to the warden. And how they had split duties between them, I do not know. Rasevic should be the guard commander, and he was responsible for the security of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have more contacts with Mr. Rasevic and Mr. Todovic than with Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I never had any contact with Mr. Krnojelac; only with Rasevic and Todovic, with Rasevic and Todovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that Mr. Todovic was a responsible clerk for assigning various jobs for the detainees. What else were his responsibilities, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And his responsibilities in assigning jobs, was that for all detainees in the prison or was it only for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Muslims and Serbs equally, because he also assigned Serbs, those who were serving long terms. He sent them to the furniture factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Rasevic or Mr. Todovic beat detainees or mistreat them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: I heard about that when that escape had happened, but I did not see that, but I also heard that they were among those who beat.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the one or the other ever threaten you or other detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, yes. Savo Todovic threatened to send me to the mine, and I told him, "Savo, you'll never live to see the day with me working in the mine."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it a threat to work in the mine, to you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was a threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to discuss with you a few staff members.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And for this purpose, I would like to have the Exhibit P55 in front of the witness -- oh, sorry. Sorry. P3, P3.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, would you please look at the person number 3, that's Milorad Krnojelac, and would you please look at the dates given in this list. You see the date 18th April 1992 to 8 September 1994. Did you see Mr. Krnojelac that long time, that is, 1994?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Sorry. It says 18th April 1992 to the 17th of July, 1992. That is what it says here on my paper. This is not right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You're on the wrong list -- sorry, you are in the wrong column, sir.

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm sorry. I am sorry. Yes, that is the correct date, 18th April 1992 to -- I think this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you see the date --

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, what kind of paper are you checking?

utterances.speaker: FWS-138
utterances.text: The one issued by the International Red Cross, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... checking on this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It may be that you need another document with a different number. Wasn't there some concession by the Prosecution in this case as to the cut-off date when Mr. Krnojelac was the warden?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but the relevance of my question is actually I want to find out with the witness the reliability of this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That is where I'm heading at.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, make sure we've got the right document. That's the next thing. You asked for P3.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, and P3 should be the list of employees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Not the Red Cross list.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, not the Red Cross list. It should be in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It may be that we had better have a look at the document he's looking at, because it may not be P3.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, would you please show me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But even with the skewed version that each of you seem to have with that clock, it's one minute to 4.00. It hardly seems worthwhile at this stage. We'll adjourn now until 9.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of January, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
